claim: Neuropathic pain is a debilitating chronic pain condition that results from injury or disease of the somatosensory system.
source: Neuropathic pain is a debilitating chronic pain condition that results from injury or disease of the somatosensory system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the definition and etiology of neuropathic pain.

claim: Chronic pain is refractory to currently available treatments.
source: Since chronic pain is refractory to currently available treatments, the development of effective treatments is a major clinical challenge (Colloca et al., 2017; Finnerup et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colloca et al., 2017 and Finnerup et al., 2021.

claim: Peripheral nerve injury causes various inflammatory responses in the nervous system that critically contribute to the development of neuropathic pain.
source: Accumulating evidence from studies using models of neuropathic pain indicates that peripheral nerve injury causes various inflammatory responses in the nervous system that critically contribute to the development of neuropathic pain (Ji et al., 2016; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ji et al., 2016 and Inoue and Tsuda, 2018.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. interleukin-1β, IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor α) are produced by various non-neuronal cells such as macrophages at injured nerves and dorsal root ganglion, and glial cells in the spinal dorsal horn.
source: Especially, pro-inflammatory cytokines [e.g. interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα)] produced by various non-neuronal cells such as macrophages at injured nerves and dorsal root ganglion (DRG), and glial cells (mainly microglia and astrocytes) in the spinal dorsal horn (SDH) modulate function of primary afferent sensory neurons and SDH neurons, leading to an increase in the excitability of pain signaling neural pathway (Ji et al., 2016; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Ji et al., 2019; Grace et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ji et al., 2016; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Ji et al., 2019; Grace et al., 2014.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines modulate function of primary afferent sensory neurons and SDH neurons, leading to an increase in the excitability of pain signaling neural pathway.
source: Especially, pro-inflammatory cytokines [e.g. interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα)] produced by various non-neuronal cells such as macrophages at injured nerves and dorsal root ganglion (DRG), and glial cells (mainly microglia and astrocytes) in the spinal dorsal horn (SDH) modulate function of primary afferent sensory neurons and SDH neurons, leading to an increase in the excitability of pain signaling neural pathway (Ji et al., 2016; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Ji et al., 2019; Grace et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ji et al., 2016; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Ji et al., 2019; Grace et al., 2014.

claim: IL-10 has a pain-relieving role and has been extensively studied in chronic pain.
source: These include IL-10, the role of which in chronic pain has been extensively studied (Vanderwall and Milligan, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanderwall and Milligan, 2019.

claim: IL-4 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine with pain-relieving effects in diverse models, including neuropathic pain.
source: Another anti-inflammatory cytokine with pain-relieving effects in diverse models, including neuropathic pain, is IL-4.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citations and discussion of IL-4's effects in various pain models.

claim: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 attenuates pain behavioral responses to bradykinin in normal animals.
source: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 has been shown to attenuate pain behavioral responses to bradykinin (Cunha et al., 1999), carrageenin (Cunha et al., 1999), TNFα (Cunha et al., 1999), zymosan (Vale et al., 2003), and acetic acid (Vale et al., 2003) in normal animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunha et al., 1999.

claim: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 attenuates pain behavioral responses to carrageenin in normal animals.
source: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 has been shown to attenuate pain behavioral responses to bradykinin (Cunha et al., 1999), carrageenin (Cunha et al., 1999), TNFα (Cunha et al., 1999), zymosan (Vale et al., 2003), and acetic acid (Vale et al., 2003) in normal animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunha et al., 1999.

claim: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 attenuates pain behavioral responses to TNFα in normal animals.
source: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 has been shown to attenuate pain behavioral responses to bradykinin (Cunha et al., 1999), carrageenin (Cunha et al., 1999), TNFα (Cunha et al., 1999), zymosan (Vale et al., 2003), and acetic acid (Vale et al., 2003) in normal animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunha et al., 1999.

claim: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 attenuates pain behavioral responses to zymosan in normal animals.
source: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 has been shown to attenuate pain behavioral responses to bradykinin (Cunha et al., 1999), carrageenin (Cunha et al., 1999), TNFα (Cunha et al., 1999), zymosan (Vale et al., 2003), and acetic acid (Vale et al., 2003) in normal animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vale et al., 2003.

claim: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 attenuates pain behavioral responses to acetic acid in normal animals.
source: Intraplantar or systemic administration of IL-4 has been shown to attenuate pain behavioral responses to bradykinin (Cunha et al., 1999), carrageenin (Cunha et al., 1999), TNFα (Cunha et al., 1999), zymosan (Vale et al., 2003), and acetic acid (Vale et al., 2003) in normal animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vale et al., 2003.

claim: Single or repeated administration of IL-4 around the injured sciatic nerve reduced behavioral pain hypersensitivity in models of neuropathic pain.
source: In models of neuropathic pain, single or repeated administration of IL-4 around the injured sciatic nerve reduced behavioral pain hypersensitivity (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015; Labuz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015; Labuz et al., 2021.

claim: The effects of IL-4 involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators.
source: These effects of IL-4 have been proposed to involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators (Kiguchi et al., 2015), polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015), increases in the production and release of IL-10 (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and opioid peptides (Celik et al., 2020; Labuz et al., 2021) from macrophages, and inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons (Nie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiguchi et al., 2015.

claim: The effects of IL-4 involve polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves.
source: These effects of IL-4 have been proposed to involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators (Kiguchi et al., 2015), polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015), increases in the production and release of IL-10 (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and opioid peptides (Celik et al., 2020; Labuz et al., 2021) from macrophages, and inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons (Nie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Celik et al., 2020 and Kiguchi et al., 2015.

claim: The effects of IL-4 involve increases in the production and release of IL-10 from macrophages.
source: These effects of IL-4 have been proposed to involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators (Kiguchi et al., 2015), polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015), increases in the production and release of IL-10 (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and opioid peptides (Celik et al., 2020; Labuz et al., 2021) from macrophages, and inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons (Nie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiguchi et al., 2015.

claim: The effects of IL-4 involve increases in the production and release of opioid peptides from macrophages.
source: These effects of IL-4 have been proposed to involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators (Kiguchi et al., 2015), polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015), increases in the production and release of IL-10 (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and opioid peptides (Celik et al., 2020; Labuz et al., 2021) from macrophages, and inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons (Nie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Celik et al., 2020 and Labuz et al., 2021.

claim: The effects of IL-4 involve inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons.
source: These effects of IL-4 have been proposed to involve a decrease in the production of inflammatory mediators (Kiguchi et al., 2015), polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype at injured nerves (Celik et al., 2020; Kiguchi et al., 2015), increases in the production and release of IL-10 (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and opioid peptides (Celik et al., 2020; Labuz et al., 2021) from macrophages, and inhibition of the increased action potentials of DRG neurons (Nie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nie et al., 2018.

claim: The central nervous system, including the spinal cord, is an important locus of action of IL-4 in pain control.
source: In addition to the diverse actions of IL-4 at the peripheral level, the central nervous system, including the spinal cord, is recognized as an important locus of action of IL-4 in pain control.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of intrathecal IL-4 effects.

claim: Intrathecal administration of IL-4 prevents the development of mechanical pain hypersensitivity in several neuropathic pain models.
source: Intrathecal administration of IL-4 prevents the development of mechanical pain hypersensitivity in several neuropathic pain models (Nie et al., 2018; Okutani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nie et al., 2018 and Okutani et al., 2018.

claim: IL-4 receptor α chain is predominantly expressed in microglia within the SDH of nerve-injured rats.
source: The target cells for the action of IL-4 intrathecally administered could be microglia since, within the SDH of nerve-injured rats, IL-4 receptor α chain (IL-4Rα) is predominantly expressed in microglia (Okutani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okutani et al., 2018.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 activates STAT6 in SDH microglia.
source: In line with this, intrathecal IL-4 activates signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6; an intracellular signal transduction molecule downstream of IL-4Rα) in SDH microglia (Okutani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okutani et al., 2018.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses cellular indexes for reactive microglia.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 or other manipulation to increase spinal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses cellular indexes for reactive microglia (Okutani et al., 2018), IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release, and microglial p38 phosphorylation (Hao et al., 2006), all of which are required to develop pain hypersensitivity (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okutani et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2006; Inoue and Tsuda, 2018.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 or other manipulation to increase spinal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses cellular indexes for reactive microglia (Okutani et al., 2018), IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release, and microglial p38 phosphorylation (Hao et al., 2006), all of which are required to develop pain hypersensitivity (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hao et al., 2006.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses microglial p38 phosphorylation.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 or other manipulation to increase spinal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses cellular indexes for reactive microglia (Okutani et al., 2018), IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release, and microglial p38 phosphorylation (Hao et al., 2006), all of which are required to develop pain hypersensitivity (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hao et al., 2006.

claim: Reactive microglia cellular indexes, IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release, and microglial p38 phosphorylation are required to develop pain hypersensitivity.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 or other manipulation to increase spinal IL-4 during the early phase after nerve injury suppresses cellular indexes for reactive microglia (Okutani et al., 2018), IL-1β and Prostaglandin E2 release, and microglial p38 phosphorylation (Hao et al., 2006), all of which are required to develop pain hypersensitivity (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue and Tsuda, 2018.

claim: Intrathecal administration of IL-4 during the late phase (e.g. 2 weeks or later after nerve injury) leads to recovery from a behavioral pain-hypersensitive state.
source: In addition to the effect of IL-4 on pain development, it is noteworthy that intrathecal administration of IL-4 during the late phase (e.g. 2 weeks or later after nerve injury) leads to recovery from a behavioral pain-hypersensitive state that develops following nerve injury (Okutani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okutani et al., 2018.

claim: The reactive states of microglia occur early after nerve injury and subside in the late phase.
source: Given that the reactive states of microglia occur early after nerve injury (e.g. cell number and expression of proinflammatory genes) and subside in the late phase (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Kohno et al., 2018; Tansley et al., 2022), it is possible that the pain-resolving effect of IL-4 involves a mechanism other than the previously reported suppression of inflammatory responses in activated microglia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Kohno et al., 2018; Tansley et al., 2022.

claim: CD11c+ microglia are necessary for the spontaneous remission of behavioral hypersensitivity associated with neuropathic pain.
source: In this study, using two different models of neuropathic pain, we demonstrated that intrathecally administered IL-4 during the late phase changes microglia to a CD11c+ state, which has recently been shown to be necessary for the spontaneous remission of behavioral hypersensitivity associated with neuropathic pain (Kohno et al., 2022), and, importantly, that this is required for the pain-relieving effect of intrathecal IL-4.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Intrathecal treatment with IL-4 increased the PWT in the hindpaw ipsilateral (but not contralateral) to the SpNT.
source: Intrathecal treatment with IL-4 increased the PWT in the hindpaw ipsilateral (but not contralateral) to the SpNT (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The behavioral remission of neuropathic mechanical hypersensitivity induced by intrathecal IL-4 persisted for at least 5 days after the last intrathecal injection.
source: Notably, this behavioral remission of neuropathic mechanical hypersensitivity persisted for at least 5 days after the last intrathecal injection of IL-4.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SpNT increased the number of Venus+ (CD11c+) cells in the SDH ipsilateral to the injury.
source: In Itgax-Venus mice, in which CD11c+ cells are visualized using the fluorescent protein Venus (Kohno et al., 2022; Lindquist et al., 2004), SpNT increased the number of Venus+ (CD11c+) cells in the SDH ipsilateral to the injury (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Almost all CD11c+ cells in the SDH after SpNT are immunohistochemically positive for IBA1 and P2Y12R.
source: Consistent with our previous data (Kohno et al., 2022), almost all CD11c+ cells were immunohistochemically positive for ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (IBA1) and the purinergic P2Y12 receptor (P2Y12R; Figure 1B and C), which are markers for myeloid cells and microglia, respectively (Butovsky et al., 2014; Ito et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, and citations to Kohno et al., 2022; Butovsky et al., 2014; Ito et al., 1998.

claim: IBA1 and P2Y12R are markers for myeloid cells and microglia, respectively.
source: Consistent with our previous data (Kohno et al., 2022), almost all CD11c+ cells were immunohistochemically positive for ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (IBA1) and the purinergic P2Y12 receptor (P2Y12R; Figure 1B and C), which are markers for myeloid cells and microglia, respectively (Butovsky et al., 2014; Ito et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Butovsky et al., 2014 and Ito et al., 1998.

claim: Intrathecal administration of IL-4 to SpNT mice enhanced the increase in CD11c+ cells in the SDH.
source: We found that intrathecal administration of IL-4 to SpNT mice enhanced the increase in CD11c+ cells in the SDH (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: CD11c+ cells increased by intrathecal IL-4 expressed both IBA1 and P2Y12R, indicating they are microglia.
source: These cells also expressed both IBA1 and P2Y12R (Figure 1B and C), indicating that CD11c+ cells increased by intrathecal IL-4 were microglia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, and inference from marker expression.

claim: Quantitative flow cytometry analysis revealed a significant increase in CD11c+ microglia in the SDH of IL-4-treated SpNT mice.
source: Quantitative flow cytometry analysis revealed a significant increase in CD11c+ microglia in the SDH of IL-4-treated SpNT mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 did not significantly change the total number of microglia in the SDH.
source: In contrast, IL-4 did not significantly change the total number of microglia in the SDH (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 did not induce infiltration of CD169+ monocytes/macrophages into the SDH.
source: In addition, intrathecal IL-4 did not induce infiltration of CD169+ monocytes/macrophages into the SDH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 also induced behavioral remission of mechanical hypersensitivity in Itgax-DTR-EGFP mice.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 also induced behavioral remission of mechanical hypersensitivity in Itgax-DTR-EGFP mice, but the pain-reducing effect was eliminated by intrathecal injection of DTX on day 17 post-SpNT (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pain-reducing effect of IL-4 was eliminated by intrathecal injection of DTX on day 17 post-SpNT in Itgax-DTR-EGFP mice.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 also induced behavioral remission of mechanical hypersensitivity in Itgax-DTR-EGFP mice, but the pain-reducing effect was eliminated by intrathecal injection of DTX on day 17 post-SpNT (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Intrathecal DTX depletes EGFP+ (CD11c+) microglia in the SDH.
source: The depletion of EGFP+ (CD11c+) microglia in the SDH by DTX injection was confirmed (Figure 2B), indicating the necessity of spinal CD11c+ microglia for the pain-relieving effect of intrathecal IL-4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spinal CD11c+ microglia are necessary for the pain-relieving effect of intrathecal IL-4.
source: The depletion of EGFP+ (CD11c+) microglia in the SDH by DTX injection was confirmed (Figure 2B), indicating the necessity of spinal CD11c+ microglia for the pain-relieving effect of intrathecal IL-4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B, demonstrating that depletion of CD11c+ microglia eliminates IL-4's pain-relieving effect.

claim: IL-4 alleviated pain hypersensitivity in female mice in a CD11c+ microglia-dependent manner.
source: IL-4 also alleviated pain hypersensitivity in female mice, which was also dependent on CD11c+ microglia (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CD11c+ cells are present at the site of injury and in the DRG.
source: In addition to SDH, CD11c+ cells have been shown to be present at the site of injury and in the DRG (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of DTX at a low dose (2 ng/g mouse) in SpNT mice treated with IL-4 on day 17 efficiently eliminated CD11c+ cells (also positive for IBA1) in the DRG on day 18.
source: The intraperitoneal administration of DTX at a low dose (2 ng/g mouse) in SpNT mice treated with IL-4 on day 17 efficiently eliminated CD11c+ cells (also positive for IBA1) in the DRG on day 18 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of DTX at a low dose did not significantly change the number of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH.
source: However, the number of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH was not significantly different between the PBS- and DTX-treated groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The elevated PWT observed in IL-4-treated mice on day 17 did not change 1 day after intraperitoneal administration of DTX.
source: Under these conditions, we found that the elevated PWT observed in IL-4-treated mice on day 17 did not change 1 day after intraperitoneal administration of DTX (day 18; Figure 4C), suggesting that CD11c+ cells in the DRG are not involved in the IL-4-induced alleviating effect on neuropathic pain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD11c+ cells in the DRG are not involved in the IL-4-induced alleviating effect on neuropathic pain.
source: Under these conditions, we found that the elevated PWT observed in IL-4-treated mice on day 17 did not change 1 day after intraperitoneal administration of DTX (day 18; Figure 4C), suggesting that CD11c+ cells in the DRG are not involved in the IL-4-induced alleviating effect on neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that selective depletion of CD11c+ cells in the DRG did not affect IL-4's pain-relieving effect.

claim: Intrathecally administered IL-4 induces spinal microglia to be in a CD11c+ state, and this induction is necessary for the ameliorating effect of IL-4 on neuropathic pain.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that intrathecally administered IL-4 induces spinal microglia to be in a CD11c+ state, and that this induction is necessary for the ameliorating effect of IL-4 on neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1-4.

claim: SNI induced a long-lasting pain-hypersensitive state without spontaneous remission, at least until day 56 post-SNI.
source: Consistent with previous data (Decosterd and Woolf, 2000), SNI induced a long-lasting pain-hypersensitive state without spontaneous remission, at least until the last day of testing (day 56 post-SNI; Figure 5A), which was in stark contrast to the time course of pain hypersensitivity in the SpNT model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Decosterd and Woolf, 2000.

claim: The number of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH at 14 days after nerve injury was lower in the SNI model than in the SpNT model.
source: We found that the number of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH at 14 days after nerve injury was lower in the SNI model than in the SpNT model (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Quantitative analysis by flow cytometry confirmed that there were fewer CD11c+ SDH microglia in the SNI mice.
source: Quantitative analysis by flow cytometry confirmed that there were fewer CD11c+ SDH microglia in the SNI mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A blunted appearance of CD11c+ microglia was observed on days 35 and 56 post-SNI.
source: A blunted appearance was also observed on days 35 and 56 post-SNI.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The total number of microglia in the SDH was comparable between the SpNT and SNI models at all time points tested.
source: In contrast, the total number of microglia in the SDH was comparable between the two models at all time points tested, suggesting an impairment of the nerve injury-induced appearance of CD11c+ microglia in the SNI model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is an impairment of the nerve injury-induced appearance of CD11c+ microglia in the SNI model.
source: In contrast, the total number of microglia in the SDH was comparable between the two models at all time points tested, suggesting an impairment of the nerve injury-induced appearance of CD11c+ microglia in the SNI model.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total microglia numbers are similar but CD11c+ microglia are reduced in SNI compared to SpNT.

claim: IGF1 is highly expressed in CD11c+ microglia and is necessary for their pain-remitting effect.
source: Furthermore, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) has been identified as a factor that is highly expressed in CD11c+ microglia and is necessary for their pain-remitting effect (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Igf1 expression in sorted microglia increased in both SpNT and SNI models after injury.
source: While Igf1 expression in sorted microglia increased in both models after injury, its levels were lower in microglia from SNI mice than in those from SpNT mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D (labeled as 6A in the figure).

claim: Igf1 expression levels in sorted microglia were lower in SNI mice than in SpNT mice.
source: While Igf1 expression in sorted microglia increased in both models after injury, its levels were lower in microglia from SNI mice than in those from SpNT mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D (labeled as 6A in the figure).

claim: An increase in Igf1 mRNA expression in the tissue homogenate of the upper half of the SDH was not observed in tissues from the SNI model.
source: In addition, an increase in Igf1 mRNA expression in the tissue homogenate of the upper half of the SDH, where CD11c+ microglia accumulate (Kohno et al., 2022), was not observed in tissues from the SNI model (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E (labeled as 6B in the figure).

claim: In FACS-isolated CD11chigh SDH microglia, the expression of Igf1 mRNA was significantly lower in the SNI model.
source: Moreover, in FACS-isolated CD11chigh SDH microglia that highly expressed IGF1, the expression of Igf1 mRNA was significantly lower in the SNI model (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F (labeled as 6C in the figure).

claim: The long-lasting pain-hypersensitive state in the SNI model could be related to the blunted increase in CD11c+ microglia in the SDH and their lower expression of IGF1.
source: Thus, given that either the depletion of CD11c+ microglia or knockout of their IGF1 prevents the spontaneous remission of pain in the SpNT model (Kohno et al., 2022), the long-lasting pain-hypersensitive state in the SNI model could be related to the blunted increase in CD11c+ microglia in the SDH and their lower expression of IGF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and previous findings cited from Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Depletion of CD11c+ microglia or knockout of their IGF1 prevents the spontaneous remission of pain in the SpNT model.
source: Thus, given that either the depletion of CD11c+ microglia or knockout of their IGF1 prevents the spontaneous remission of pain in the SpNT model (Kohno et al., 2022), the long-lasting pain-hypersensitive state in the SNI model could be related to the blunted increase in CD11c+ microglia in the SDH and their lower expression of IGF1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Intrathecal treatment with IL-4 in SNI mice from day 14 to day 16 significantly increased the number of CD11c+ microglia on day 21.
source: Intrathecal treatment with IL-4 in SNI mice from day 14 to day 16 significantly increased the number of CD11c+ microglia on day 21, almost all of which were positive for IBA1 and P2Y12R (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Almost all CD11c+ microglia increased by IL-4 in SNI mice were positive for IBA1 and P2Y12R.
source: Intrathecal treatment with IL-4 in SNI mice from day 14 to day 16 significantly increased the number of CD11c+ microglia on day 21, almost all of which were positive for IBA1 and P2Y12R (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The total number of microglia in the SDH was not significantly different between PBS- and IL-4-treated SNI mice.
source: Similar to the data obtained for SpNT mice, the total number of microglia in the SDH was not significantly different between PBS- and IL-4-treated SNI mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 treatment alleviated the SNI-induced mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Behaviorally, intrathecal IL-4 treatment alleviated the SNI-induced mechanical hypersensitivity (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The depletion of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH of IL-4-treated SNI mice by intrathecal administration of DTX on day 17 negated the ameliorating effect of IL-4 on pain hypersensitivity.
source: Furthermore, the depletion of CD11c+ microglia in the SDH of IL-4-treated SNI mice by intrathecal administration of DTX on day 17 negated the ameliorating effect of IL-4 on pain hypersensitivity (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The IL-4's pain-relieving effect was not observed in Cx3cr1CreERT2/+;Igf1flox/flox mice treated with tamoxifen.
source: Moreover, the IL-4's effect was not observed in Cx3cr1CreERT2/+;Igf1flox/flox mice treated with tamoxifen (Figure 8C), a treatment that enables selective knockout of the Igf1 gene in tissue-resident Cx3cr1+ cells (Parkhurst et al., 2013), the majority of which are microglia in the SDH (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and citations to Parkhurst et al., 2013 and Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Intrathecally administered IL-4 exhibited a pain-remitting effect in the SNI model, which was dependent on CD11c+ microglia and IGF1.
source: Overall, intrathecally administered IL-4 exhibited a pain-remitting effect in the SNI model, which was dependent on CD11c+ microglia and IGF1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Following peripheral nerve injury, microglia in the SDH cause significant changes in morphology, cell number, transcriptional and translational activities, and function.
source: Increasing evidence indicates that following peripheral nerve injury, microglia in the SDH cause significant changes in morphology, cell number, transcriptional and translational activities, and function (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Tansley et al., 2022; Shibata et al., 2025; Masuda et al., 2012; Masuda et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Tansley et al., 2022; Shibata et al., 2025; Masuda et al., 2012; Masuda et al., 2014.

claim: Microglial changes occurring in the early phase after nerve injury are necessary for the development of neuropathic pain.
source: Numerous studies have shown that these changes occurring in the early phase after nerve injury are necessary for the development of neuropathic pain (Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Masuda et al., 2012; Masuda et al., 2014; Tsuda et al., 2003; Coull et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Inoue and Tsuda, 2018; Masuda et al., 2012; Masuda et al., 2014; Tsuda et al., 2003; Coull et al., 2005.

claim: Some SDH microglia in the later phase are changed into CD11c+ states with different transcriptional and functional profiles.
source: In contrast to their role, we have recently shown that some SDH microglia in the later phase are changed into CD11c+ states with different transcriptional and functional profiles and that these microglia are required for spontaneous remission of neuropathic pain (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: CD11c+ microglia are required for spontaneous remission of neuropathic pain.
source: In contrast to their role, we have recently shown that some SDH microglia in the later phase are changed into CD11c+ states with different transcriptional and functional profiles and that these microglia are required for spontaneous remission of neuropathic pain (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: CD11c+ microglia are an essential target of IL-4 administered intrathecally to induce the behavioral remission of pain hypersensitivity.
source: In this study, we demonstrated for the first time that CD11c+ microglia are an essential target of IL-4 administered intrathecally to induce the behavioral remission of pain hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The pharmacological effect of intrathecal IL-4 appears to be mediated by its direct action on spinal microglia.
source: The pharmacological effect of intrathecal IL-4 appears to be mediated by its direct action on spinal microglia, as the expression of IL-4Rα in the SDH has been shown to be predominant in microglia after nerve injury (Okutani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the citation to Okutani et al., 2018 showing IL-4Rα expression in microglia.

claim: Activation of STAT6 after intrathecal IL-4 selectively occurs in spinal microglia.
source: This is also supported by the data that activation of STAT6 (the downstream molecule of IL-4Rα) after intrathecal IL-4 selectively occurs in spinal microglia (Okutani et al., 2018) and that primary cultured microglia treated with IL-4 become CD11c+ and express IGF1 (Butovsky et al., 2006; Chiu et al., 2008; Butovsky et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okutani et al., 2018.

claim: Primary cultured microglia treated with IL-4 become CD11c+ and express IGF1.
source: This is also supported by the data that activation of STAT6 (the downstream molecule of IL-4Rα) after intrathecal IL-4 selectively occurs in spinal microglia (Okutani et al., 2018) and that primary cultured microglia treated with IL-4 become CD11c+ and express IGF1 (Butovsky et al., 2006; Chiu et al., 2008; Butovsky et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Butovsky et al., 2006; Chiu et al., 2008; Butovsky et al., 2005.

claim: IL-4 acts on microglia and changes their state to CD11c+ microglia (rather than the proliferation of CD11c+ microglia themselves).
source: Furthermore, based on our data showing that IL-4 increased the number of CD11c+ microglia without affecting the total number of microglia, it is conceivable that IL-4 acts on microglia and changes their state to CD11c+ microglia (rather than the proliferation of CD11c+ microglia themselves), leading to behavioral remission of neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased CD11c+ microglia without change in total microglia numbers.

claim: Intrathecal IL-4 administration increased CD11c+ microglia in the SDH contralateral to SpNT but did not change the PWT in the contralateral hindpaw.
source: Intrathecal IL-4 administration also increased CD11c+ microglia in the SDH contralateral to SpNT but did not change the PWT in the contralateral hindpaw.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The selective effect of CD11c+ microglia on pathologically heightened pain sensitivity explains why IL-4 increases CD11c+ microglia contralaterally without affecting contralateral PWT.
source: This gap seems to be related to the selective effect of CD11c+ microglia and their factors (especially IGF1) on pathologically heightened pain sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD11c+ microglia only affect pathological pain states.

claim: Depletion of CD11c+ spinal microglia and intrathecal administration of IGF1 do not elevate pain threshold of the contralateral hindpaw.
source: In fact, depletion of CD11c+ spinal microglia and intrathecal administration of IGF1 do not elevate pain threshold of the contralateral hindpaw (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: IL-4 applied to injured peripheral nerves, such as sciatic nerves, ameliorates neuropathic mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: IL-4 applied to injured peripheral nerves, such as sciatic nerves, ameliorates neuropathic mechanical hypersensitivity (Kiguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiguchi et al., 2015.

claim: IL-4Rα expression is upregulated in macrophages that accumulate in injured sciatic nerves.
source: In sciatic nerves, IL-4Rα expression is upregulated in macrophages that accumulate in injured nerves (Kiguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiguchi et al., 2015.

claim: CCR2+ monocytes were increased in the capsule of the DRG after IL-4 treatment.
source: Intrathecally administered IL-4 may affect cells in the DRG, since chemokine (C-C motif) receptor 2 (CCR2)+ monocytes were increased in the capsule of the DRG after IL-4 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cells required for intrathecal IL-4 to ameliorate pain hypersensitivity are CD11c+ microglia in the SDH, but not peripheral CD11c+ macrophages.
source: However, our findings obtained from mice with depletion of CD11c+ IBA1+ cells (presumably macrophages) in the DRG (but not SDH) suggest that the cells required for intrathecal IL-4 to ameliorate pain hypersensitivity are CD11c+ microglia in the SDH, but not peripheral CD11c+ macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that peripheral CD11c+ cell depletion does not affect IL-4's pain-relieving effect.

claim: Perineurally administered IL-4 can act on macrophages, which leads to a change in their state from pro- to anti-inflammatory via a STAT6-dependent mechanism.
source: Furthermore, perineurally administered IL-4 can act on macrophages, which leads to a change in their state from pro- to anti-inflammatory via a STAT6-dependent mechanism (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and further to a release of opioid peptides that are key factors in the suppression of neuropathic pain (Celik et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiguchi et al., 2015 and Celik et al., 2020.

claim: Opioid peptides released from macrophages are key factors in the suppression of neuropathic pain.
source: Furthermore, perineurally administered IL-4 can act on macrophages, which leads to a change in their state from pro- to anti-inflammatory via a STAT6-dependent mechanism (Kiguchi et al., 2015) and further to a release of opioid peptides that are key factors in the suppression of neuropathic pain (Celik et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Celik et al., 2020.

claim: IGF1 is necessary for the pain-relieving effect of CD11c+ microglia induced by IL-4 in the SDH.
source: In the SDH, IGF1 appears to be necessary for the pain-relieving effect of CD11c+ microglia induced by IL-4.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from IGF1-knockout mice shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Igf1 expression is much higher in CD11c+ microglia than in CD11cneg microglia.
source: Although Cx3cr1+ cells, other than CD11c+ microglia, also lack Igf1 in these mice, given Igf1 expression is much higher in CD11c+ microglia than in CD11cneg microglia (Kohno et al., 2022), IGF1 from CD11c+ microglia would play an important role in IL-4-induced pain remission.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: IGF1 from CD11c+ microglia plays an important role in IL-4-induced pain remission.
source: Although Cx3cr1+ cells, other than CD11c+ microglia, also lack Igf1 in these mice, given Igf1 expression is much higher in CD11c+ microglia than in CD11cneg microglia (Kohno et al., 2022), IGF1 from CD11c+ microglia would play an important role in IL-4-induced pain remission.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and the citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: The molecular basis of IL-4's ameliorating effects on neuropathic pain hypersensitivity is different between macrophages in the DRG/injured nerves and microglia in the SDH.
source: Thus, while IL-4 acts on macrophages and microglia in the DRG/injured nerves and the SDH, respectively, the molecular basis of its ameliorating effects on neuropathic pain hypersensitivity is different.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of different mechanisms (opioid peptides peripherally vs. IGF1 centrally).

claim: The emergence of CD11c+ spinal microglia following nerve injury was impaired in the SNI model.
source: Another notable finding of this study was that the emergence of CD11c+ spinal microglia following nerve injury was impaired in the SNI model, which did not exhibit spontaneous remission of behavioral pain hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The reduced ability of spinal microglia to shift toward the CD11c+ state in the SNI model contributes to long-lasting pain hypersensitivity.
source: This raises the possibility that the reduced ability of spinal microglia to shift toward the CD11c+ state in the SNI model contributes, at least in part, to long-lasting pain hypersensitivity because SpNT mice with depleted CD11c+ spinal microglia have been shown to exhibit persistent pain hypersensitivity (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: SpNT mice with depleted CD11c+ spinal microglia exhibit persistent pain hypersensitivity.
source: This raises the possibility that the reduced ability of spinal microglia to shift toward the CD11c+ state in the SNI model contributes, at least in part, to long-lasting pain hypersensitivity because SpNT mice with depleted CD11c+ spinal microglia have been shown to exhibit persistent pain hypersensitivity (Kohno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohno et al., 2022.

claim: Spinal microglia in the SNI model retain the ability to respond to IL-4, allowing microglia to be in a CD11c+ state that remits neuropathic pain.
source: These data suggest that spinal microglia in the SNI model retain the ability to respond to IL-4, allowing microglia to be in a CD11c+ state that remits neuropathic pain and broadly extends their therapeutic potential to neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing IL-4 can induce CD11c+ microglia and pain relief in SNI model.

claim: CD8+ T cells infiltrating into spinal cord have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
source: Recent studies have also indicated that immune cells such as CD8+ T cells infiltrating into spinal cord (Fan et al., 2025), and regulatory T cells (Kuhn et al., 2021; Midavaine et al., 2025) and MRC1+ macrophages (Niehaus et al., 2021) in the spinal meninges have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2025.

claim: Regulatory T cells in the spinal meninges have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
source: Recent studies have also indicated that immune cells such as CD8+ T cells infiltrating into spinal cord (Fan et al., 2025), and regulatory T cells (Kuhn et al., 2021; Midavaine et al., 2025) and MRC1+ macrophages (Niehaus et al., 2021) in the spinal meninges have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuhn et al., 2021 and Midavaine et al., 2025.

claim: MRC1+ macrophages in the spinal meninges have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
source: Recent studies have also indicated that immune cells such as CD8+ T cells infiltrating into spinal cord (Fan et al., 2025), and regulatory T cells (Kuhn et al., 2021; Midavaine et al., 2025) and MRC1+ macrophages (Niehaus et al., 2021) in the spinal meninges have important roles in controlling microglial states and neuropathic pain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Niehaus et al., 2021.

claim: IL-4 increases CD11c+ microglia without affecting the total number of microglia.
source: Furthermore, our data, demonstrating that IL-4 increases CD11c+ microglia without affecting the total number of microglia, could open a new avenue for developing strategies to modulate microglial subpopulations through molecular targeting, which may lead to new analgesics.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 7.

claim: CD11c+ microglia have been implicated in Alzheimer disease.
source: Moreover, since CD11c+ microglia have been implicated in other CNS diseases (e.g. Alzheimer disease Keren-Shaul et al., 2017, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Xie et al., 2022, and multiple sclerosis Wlodarczyk et al., 2018), further investigations into the mechanisms driving CD11c+ microglia induction could provide insights into novel therapeutic strategies not only for neuropathic pain but also for other CNS diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Keren-Shaul et al., 2017.

claim: CD11c+ microglia have been implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Moreover, since CD11c+ microglia have been implicated in other CNS diseases (e.g. Alzheimer disease Keren-Shaul et al., 2017, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Xie et al., 2022, and multiple sclerosis Wlodarczyk et al., 2018), further investigations into the mechanisms driving CD11c+ microglia induction could provide insights into novel therapeutic strategies not only for neuropathic pain but also for other CNS diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2022.

source: Moreover, since CD11c+ microglia have been implicated in other CNS diseases (e.g. Alzheimer disease Keren-Shaul et al., 2017, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Xie et al., 2022, and multiple sclerosis Wlodarczyk et al., 2018), further investigations into the mechanisms driving CD11c+ microglia induction could provide insights into novel therapeutic strategies not only for neuropathic pain but also for other CNS diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wlodarczyk et al., 2018.
